1. PH3 (phosphine) has a phosphorus atom bonded to three hydrogen atoms. The phosphorus has 5 valence electrons, with three used in bonds to hydrogen and two remaining as a lone pair. This gives a tetrahedral electron arrangement with sp³ hybridization.

2. [PH4]+ is formed when PH3 accepts a proton (H+), which bonds to the lone pair of electrons on phosphorus. In [PH4]+, all four sp³ hybrid orbitals of phosphorus are now used for bonding with hydrogen atoms, with no lone pairs remaining.

3. According to VSEPR theory, lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs, causing greater repulsion. This means:
   - In PH3, the lone pair repels the bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs repel each other
   - This stronger repulsion pushes the bonding pairs closer together, decreasing the H-P-H bond angles (typically around 93-94° instead of the ideal tetrahedral 109.5°)
   - In [PH4]+, with no lone pairs, all four P-H bonds repel each other equally, resulting in a perfect tetrahedral arrangement with bond angles of 109.5°

Therefore, even though both molecules have sp³ hybridization, the bond angles in [PH4]+ are larger than in PH3 because of the absence of the lone pair that causes stronger repulsion in PH3.
